## TL;DR

Tightened boot-time preview orphan detection so it no longer treats a process as ours merely because its command line contains the preview executable's basename. When the port is absent from the `ps` output, detection now requires a complete second command token as well as the executable basename. I verified the relevant `shell: true` behavior on this macOS host and ran the requested scoped RepoOS check.

## Work and rationale

The failure mode in #0363 was a PID reuse collision: after the server crashed, a different process could inherit a preview PID. The previous fallback accepted any `ps` command line containing the recorded binary basename. A preview recorded as `bun ...` could therefore claim an unrelated `bun test` process.

I kept the existing exact `--port <port>` match as the first signal. When that signal is missing, the code tokenizes the beginning of the recorded launch command, taking shell-quoted strings as single tokens, and checks the process command line for the executable basename and the full second token at a whitespace boundary. This adds a distinguishing argument without relying on a particular command shape or introducing environment plumbing and registry changes. Commands containing only a binary name and no visible port now fail closed.

The matcher remains intentionally based on command-line evidence because the current persisted preview record has no process nonce. The implementation does not alter launch behavior, process-group handling, or legacy structural matching for records without a custom command.

## Approaches tried

I considered adding a unique child environment marker. That would avoid command-line parsing, but it would require a reliable way to query a specific process's environment across supported operating systems and account for that marker in persisted records and spawn paths. For this narrow follow-up, a second argv token makes a focused change while retaining the existing `ps` inspection.

I also considered matching a longer normalized command prefix. Shell quoting and path rendering complicate a full prefix comparison: `ps` strips quote delimiters and may show executable paths differently. Requiring the first argument token to appear whole avoids treating an argument substring as a match, while remaining tolerant of quote removal.

## Challenges and blockers

The requested real platform check could be performed only on macOS in this session. A live detached process launched with `shell: true` was inspected using `ps -p <pid> -o command=`; macOS showed the executed command (`bun -e ...`) for the spawned PID. Linux was not available in this environment, so I have not claimed a Linux observation. The matching rule uses whitespace-delimited command-line tokens and avoids shell-wrapper-specific assumptions, but Linux behavior still needs confirmation in an environment that can run it.

## Key learnings

The original fallback was materially broader than the recorded command: a binary name is common and does not establish process identity. A complete argument token is a better distinguishing signal for the commands this registry stores, while exact port matching remains preferred when available. `shell: true` does not necessarily mean the PID inspected by `ps` will remain a shell wrapper; the actual macOS behavior observed here was the executed Bun command.
